title: Aamir Khan Is Getting Married on July 5. The Man Who Once Called Wedding-at-60 'Inappropriate' Found His Contentment After All.
excerpt: A quarter-century friendship turned romance, a navy-blue co-ord at the Mumbai airport, and a registered marriage at home. Inside the most low-key superstar wedding of the year.
body:
It happened in the quiet hours of a Thursday morning, the kind of arrival that usually slips past unnoticed. But there is no slipping past for **Aamir Khan**. The cameras were waiting at the Mumbai airport, and out he came — black tee, black trousers, the signature spectacles, a cap pulled low — holding the hand of the woman he is about to marry. **Gauri Spratt** walked beside him in a navy-blue co-ord, unhurried, smiling, entirely at ease. He pulled his mask off in a rush, turned to the swarm of paparazzi, and said the most disarming thing a 61-year-old superstar could say on his way to a wedding: *"Arey, beti ko ghar leke jaana hai yaar, please."* I have to take my daughter home.

That is the register of this entire affair — tender, unbothered, almost defiantly ordinary for a man whose every move is a headline.

> "Salman has loved what he's heard" is the kind of sentence Bollywood runs on. "I've found contentment" is the kind Aamir Khan now says about his own life.

The date is set. According to Filmfare, which first broke the story and has since been confirmed by Aamir himself, the couple will tie the knot on **July 5, 2026**, in an intimate ceremony — a simple registered marriage at home, in the presence of family and a tight circle of friends. No baraat that shuts down a suburb, no five-day spectacle leaked frame by frame to the press. For one of the three Khans who have defined Hindi cinema for three decades, it is a remarkably small door to walk through into a third marriage.

And it is the *third* that makes this story land the way it does. This is the same Aamir Khan who, not so long ago, called the idea of marrying at 60 "inappropriate." The same man who has spoken with unusual candour about the unraveling of two marriages — to **Reena Dutta**, the mother of his children, and to **Kiran Rao**, his creative partner and the director of *Laagaan*-era ambition. He once admitted it took him four years to heal after the first divorce. He has said, plainly, that he is grateful to have known the women he loved, even when it didn't last.

What's striking is that none of those bridges seem to have burned. In the lead-up to the July wedding, Gauri has reportedly been spotted spending easy, warm time with Kiran Rao herself — the ex-wife and the wife-to-be, sharing a room, sharing a moment. In an industry that loves a feud, the absence of one is its own kind of glamour.

Gauri Spratt is not a newcomer to Aamir's life. The two are said to have known each other for nearly **25 years** before friendship tipped into romance — a slow burn that finally went public when Aamir, in a move both old-fashioned and oddly sweet, introduced her to the press during his 60th birthday celebrations earlier this year. Since then she has been a steady presence: at film festivals, at family holidays, at airport gates. At the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne. On a New Year's getaway with nephew Imran Khan and Aamir's 90-year-old mother in tow. The Khan family, in full.

The timing carries its own weight. The appearance comes amid a public family rift with Aamir's brother **Faissal Khan**, who has made pointed accusations against his siblings — a drama the family has firmly pushed back on. That Aamir and Gauri have moved through this stretch hand-in-hand, refusing to perform crisis for the cameras, says something about the footing they've found.

There's a professional crescendo here too. Aamir is fresh off *Sitaare Zameen Par*, the spiritual sequel to *Taare Zameen Par*, and is gearing up for the Rajinikanth-led *Coolie* — a film he reportedly signed without hearing the script, just to share a frame with the Superstar. A man at the height of his second wind, walking into a marriage he once swore off.

For the diaspora watching from New Jersey to Southall to Brampton, there is something quietly moving about this one. We grew up on Aamir — the perfectionist, the box-office strategist, the actor who made his blockbusters mean something. To watch him, at 61, choose a small wedding and a woman he's known for half his life, is to watch a certain kind of stardom soften into something human.

The ceremony will be private. The pictures, if there are any, will be few. But the story — the friend who became the love, the contentment found late, the families that stayed kind — is the most romantic thing Bollywood has handed us all year. And it isn't even a film.
